snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew verb shalach ('to send') appears repeatedly throughout 2 Samuel 11 as David's tool of manipulation—sending for Bathsheba, sending Uriah to battle, sending the sealed letter ordering his death. This vocabulary choice transforms David from a direct actor into a remote manipulator, extending his power through agents rather than taking responsibility himself.

Solomon's prayer at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:9) requests not long life, wealth, or military victory—the typical petitions of ancient rulers—but a 'listening heart' to discern good from evil. This selfless request for wisdom to serve God's people becomes the foundation for all his subsequent blessings, including the wisdom to build the Temple.

In Solomon's famous judgment (1 Kings 3:26), the true mother's 'compassion burned fiercely'—using a Hebrew verb (nikhmeru) derived from 'womb,' describing an involuntary, physically rooted maternal response. Her willingness to surrender her child to save his life reveals truth that no external witness could establish.

Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:1-6) uses the identical Hebrew verb (laqach, 'to take') that Samuel warned against in his description of kingly tyranny (1 Samuel 8:11-17). David, who swore to protect Israel from such exploitation, becomes the very predatory king Samuel predicted—taking what belongs to another through his power.

The Temple's purpose, stated directly by the Lord (1 Kings 6:13), is not the building itself but divine presence: 'I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will not forsake my people.' In Latter-day Saint covenant theology, this echoes the fundamental promise that through temple ordinances, God will never abandon those who keep their covenants.

Uriah's refusal to enjoy comfort while soldiers are in the field (2 Samuel 11:11) names the Ark of the Covenant first in his principled explanation—showing that covenant loyalty transcends personal desire. His sacrifice of conjugal rights prefigures the temple principle that all personal interests must be consecrated to God's purposes.
